description: Shackleton Station: a pre-formed team of friends from the DC/Maryland area tackling the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge. We’re building a tool to plan lunar south pole landings, showing when the Sun is up for power and when Earth is visible for comms, using NASA data. Skills: satellite data and Python, software engineering, frontend/map visualization, and presentation. Good luck!
summary:
Sightline is a web tool that answers one question for a Moon mission: where to land, and when. At the Moon's south pole the Sun and Earth barely clear the horizon, so a nearby ridge can cut off power or radio contact, and a small change of place or date can flip the answer. Five missions have aimed for the region; one landed cleanly.

Pick a site, a landing date and a mission, and Sightline returns a verdict: this landing fits, fits with little margin, or does not, and why. If the schedule slips, it finds the next landing that fits. If the lander misses its mark, it shows how much error the mission can survive and a better place to aim. It shows the Sun and Earth over the real skyline hour by hour, compares up to four sites or dates side by side, and has a built-in AI guide, Scout, for questions in plain words.

Every number is computed from NASA terrain and ephemeris data: 1.04 trillion Sun and Earth answers covering every hour from 2026 through 2049, with positions checked against JPL Horizons to within 0.01°. Sightline turns specialist analysis into answers that planners, educators and students can read in seconds.
details:
Source code: https://github.com/shackleton-station/sightline

Live site: https://lunarsightline.com

The problem

Missions are heading to the Moon's south pole for its water ice and its long stretches of sunlight. It is also the hardest place to land. The Sun and Earth barely clear the horizon there, so a nearby ridge can cut off power or radio contact, and a small change of place or date can flip the answer.

Five missions have aimed for the region, and one landed cleanly. Chandrayaan-3 (2023) touched down soon after local sunrise and worked for about 11 days. Odysseus (2024) tipped over, but came to rest in sunlight and in contact with Earth, and returned data for about a week. Athena (2025) also tipped over, about 250 meters off target in a shadowed crater, and died within a day.

Those landings show what a plan has to get right. Sunlight and a radio link decide survival. The landing hour decides how much daylight is left. A few hundred meters can be the difference between a lit plateau and a dark crater. NASA's tools hold the data to check all of this, but each answers one part of the question at a time.

What it does

Sightline checks a landing plan on one screen.

  • A verdict. Pick a site, a landing date and hour, and a mission. Sightline answers "fits", "fits with little margin" or "does not fit", and says why, with the Sun's elevation, the hours of sunlight, the windows of contact with Earth, and the time left until sunset and Earthset.
  • Any site. Thirteen are listed: Apollo landings, NASA's commercial landers, other countries' landers and the south pole's ridge sites. Any other point on the Moon can be entered by its coordinates.
  • Any mission. A mission is a set of limits: how long it stays, the longest dark and the longest radio silence it can survive, whether it needs the Sun and Earth at touchdown, the steepest ground, and how far Earth must clear the skyline for a dependable link. There are presets, one of them based on Canada's lunar utility rover.
  • When the date slips. If a landing does not fit, one press gives the next one that does. The Planner shows every listed site against every month, for any year through 2049, and counts the days with a landing that fits.
  • When the landing misses. Landing accuracy simulates touchdowns around the aim point and shows what share still fit, what goes wrong in the rest, and a better place to aim. At Connecting Ridge on 22 June 2027, 38% of touchdowns within about 100 m fit; moving the aim 44 m raises that to 60%.
  • Side by side. Up to four sites or dates are compared row by row, with the best value in each row marked. There is no blended score: the trade-offs belong to the planner.
  • Seeing it. The same hour from orbit, from above the site, and from the surface, where the Sun and Earth stand over the real skyline. A time bar plays the mission hour by hour, or steps out to a month or a year.
  • For everyone. A guided tour follows one landing plan across the screen, a Guide explains the south pole from the start, and Scout, a built-in AI guide, answers questions in plain words. A plan can be shared as a link or printed as a brief.

How it works

  1. Terrain. NASA's LOLA laser altimeter gives the shape of the ground: 20 m per pixel across the south pole, and 5 m at the main ridge sites.
  2. Skyline. From each point the terrain is traced outward in 720 directions over a curved Moon. The result is the outline of the land as a lander would see it.
  3. Sun and Earth. NASA's SPICE data gives their positions for every hour from 2026 through 2049, including the monthly wobble that carries Earth up and down at the pole.
  4. The check. For each hour, how much of each disc is above that skyline. With no air to soften it, the skyline is a hard edge.

The same calculation runs at 2.5 million points around the pole. In all, Sightline computes 1.04 trillion Sun and Earth answers from 21 GB of NASA terrain. They are computed ahead of time, so a visitor's answer arrives at once.

How we know it is right

  • Positions. Every hourly Sun and Earth position matches JPL Horizons to within 0.01°, in 5,469,984 checks.
  • Sunlight. Long-run sunlight is within 1.2 percentage points of NASA's illumination maps on average, across more than a million points.
  • Photos. Against 235 dated photos taken from orbit, the model calls 92% of the clear ones right.

Where Sightline and NASA disagree, the site says so, and the Guide lists what Sightline cannot tell you. Scout is held to the same standard: the AI never writes a number, and Sightline's own code fills in every figure.

Benefits and impact

A mission planner can test a landing plan in seconds, in place of working through three specialist tools, and can see at once what a slipped launch date or a missed landing does to it. Science and engineering teams can pass the same plan between them as a link or a printed brief. Students and the public get the same answer in plain words. Sightline is free, needs no account to use, and its source code is public.

How it is creative

  • A verdict, not only a chart: a landing fits the mission, fits with little margin, or does not, and Sightline says why.
  • The next answer before it is asked: when a landing does not fit, Sightline names the next one that does.
  • What a miss changes: it simulates touchdowns around the aim point and offers a better place to aim.
  • An AI guide that cannot make up a number: Scout looks answers up, and the server fills in every figure.
  • One hour, three views: from orbit, from above the site and from the surface, over the real skyline.

What we considered

Scientific validity came first: every figure is computed from NASA data and checked against NASA three ways. Then ease of use for people who are not specialists: one screen, plain words, and the answer before the detail. Then honesty about AI: Scout may look things up and explain them, and may not invent a number. Last, speed: results are computed ahead of time, so nobody waits.

Tools and technology

  • NASA data. LOLA terrain, NAIF SPICE kernels, JPL Horizons, NASA's illumination maps and LROC photos (used to test the results), and Moon Trek and LROC Quickmap (map layers, and links out for deeper analysis).
  • Pipeline. Python with SpiceyPy, NumPy, Numba, Rasterio and PyProj.
  • Web app. TypeScript and React, Three.js (WebGL) for the 3D Moon and the surface view, D3 for the timelines.
  • Hosting. Node.js with Hono on Google Cloud Run, Cloud Storage and Cloud CDN, Redis and Firestore, all defined in Terraform and released through GitHub Actions.
  • AI. Claude (Anthropic) powers Scout, which can only call Sightline's own read-only lookups. Claude Code, an SI tool, was used to write and review code under the team's direction, as recorded in the repository's AI_USAGE.md and in commit messages. The narration of the demo and of the tour is an AI-generated voice (Google Cloud Text-to-Speech), and Scout's mark was drawn with AI. Both are labeled.
